The development objective of the Governance Modernization to Enable Efficient Service Delivery Project for Ethiopia is to improve government institutional capacity to mobilize and manage public financial and human resources efficiently. scope_basis: Research on digital repression of women.
title: Gender and Digital Repression: The Practice and Toll of Digital Repression on Women in the Authoritarian Turn
description: This project analyses the gendered dimensions of digital repression and their impact in Ethiopia and Zimbabwe. Women experience unequal access to the Internet, which impacts their socio-economic opportunities and health. This digital gender divide transcends all aspects of the online ecosystem, but there has been little exploration of how it manifests in authoritarian states where digital rights are under threat. Digital repression involves controlling, surveying, silencing, and/or punishing certain online narratives deemed a threat to the state. It involves those in power mediating the relationship between citizens and internet technologies and the state using digital tools against their citizens. Across the African continent, digital repression tactics are becoming normalised as part of the autocratic states' repertoire of ruling, demanding an interrogation of strategies states use to suppress their populace and its consequences. Specifically, it requires an intersectional exploration of the digital gender divide in authoritarian states.

title: Strengthening the management and sharing of research data
description: Governments, research funders, scholarly publishers, and academic organizations are increasingly advocating for greater openness to research data to catalyze innovation and collaboration and to uphold research integrity by allowing others to query or build on research findings. While these rationales are compelling, the management, curation, and archiving of research data in open repositories is not established practice in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. This project seeks to strengthen the management and sharing of research data generated through IDRC-funded research projects. The project will invite researchers funded by IDRC to participate in a peer-learning process that will result in their data being archived in appropriate data repositories. This will involve the development of data management plans, papers describing their data, and the curation of datasets. The process will be guided by international advisors who will help researchers understand the administrative process, ethical considerations, and data curation techniques that support the archiving of research data in open repositories. As researcher practices and infrastructures vary across regions, the project will convene workshops in Africa, Asia, and South America to exchange experiences in the management and sharing of research data in each region. Insights from peer exchanges and guidance provided by the international advisors will be used by researchers to publish their data papers and archive their data. IDRC staff will contribute to and learn from these peer-learning processes to improve the guidance the Centre provides to grantees in support of its Open Data Statement of Principles.

scope_basis: Research on civil registration for displaced women and children.
title: Centre of Excellence for CRVS Systems: The vulnerability of internally displaced women and children whose civil status is not registered in Ethiopia
description: Emergencies and displacements create major challenges to the provision of effective civil registration services such as marriages, births, and deaths. Restoring registration activities and clearing backlogs after emergencies are often complex and costly undertakings requiring specific legal, operational, and policy provisions. Civil registration is a critical tool for protecting fundamental human rights and freedoms. When civil registration systems fail due to conflicts and emergencies, people are unable to register vital events or obtain proof of identity and civil status. Without this proof, they are unable to access critical social services such as health, education, and social welfare. This can have catastrophic consequences for women and children, who are especially vulnerable to gender-based and sexual violence in situations of conflict and fragility, and who are the first victims of conflict. Without proof of civil status or legal identity, they are even more vulnerable because they are unable to access the social services they need, nor can they prove links to their countries of origin. Proving these links is key in order to return to their countries of origin or to be relocated to another safe country by mandated United Nations agencies. This project is supported under the Centre of Excellence for Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) Systems, a joint initiative of IDRC and Global Affairs Canada. With the collaboration of Addis Ababa University, the project will assess the existing legal and policy environment related to CRVS and examine the effect of civil registration status on the vulnerability of women and children displaced due to ethnic conflicts in Ethiopia. This study will examine the impact of the lack of documentation on access to humanitarian and other essential services, as well as vulnerability to sexual abuse, food insecurity, poor health, school dropouts, and conflict with the host population over resources. Previous studies on the subject have either examined the importance of identity documentation or the vulnerability of internally displaced populations, but few have considered the link between access to identity documentation and vulnerability. This will, therefore, be an important contribution to the field. Expected outputs include a peer-reviewed publication and a high-level synthesis report that will be presented to the Civil Registration Technical Advisory Group to propose legislative modifications for internally displaced population-facilitated registration.

scope_basis: Launch of a shared mobile money platform.
title: Ethiopia - Capacity building for financial inclusion in Ethiopia (M-BIRR Mobile Money)
description: The project is anchored with Pillar I of the Bank’s new Financial Sector Development Strategy. This pillar aims at increasing access to financial services to the underserved through technology. The project is also in line with the Bank’s operational focus on financial intermediation and microfinance as well as supporting MSMEs. The project aims to advance financial inclusion and improve the efficiency of the participating five Ethiopian MFIs in Ethiopia with the launch of a shared mobile money platform (M-Birr Mobile Money Service), and the development of an agent network that will expand the reach of the MFIs and formal financial services in general in Ethiopia. It will increase the proportion of poor households and small businesses with access to formal financial services. It will also deepen the financial sector infrastructure and promote the 5MFIs inclusive microfinance model that works for the poor. The total FAPA grant proposed to cover up the launch of the M-Birr Mobile Money Service is for USD 318,000. The project’s objective is to successfully launch M-Birr Mobile Money Service, to be used by the five MFI shareholders, through the newly established AODAO Inclusive Finance Technology Share Company (ShareCo). The ShareCo will be responsible for the operation of the M-Birr platform and brand, and for deploying the training of MFIs staff and agents in the use and provision of M-Birr Mobile Money Service. The launch is to be carried out over a period of (9) months, by initially deploying 1,011 branches and 3,033 agents. With branches and agents, MFIs will be able to reach a larger number of clients farther away from their branches, and offer them efficient and reliable mobile money service. M-Birr Mobile Money service is initially deployed within five regions in Ethiopia, namely, Tigray, Amhara, Addis Ababa, Oromia, and SNNP. Precisely, the project’s beneficiaries will be (i) new clients who, in absence of formal banking services, use more expensive or riskier informal financial services (ii) MFIs who will be enabled to roll out banking services beyond their bricks and mortar network, and (iii) mobile money agents who can develop new revenue streams and create new jobs.
